# Rebuilding GFDS from scratch {#sec-gfds-rebuild}

---
jupyter: ds-flood-gfm
---

@sec-alternative-sources showed that JRC's Global Flood Detection System
(GFDS) tracks riverine floods at admin level about as well as FloodScan, for
free. Then the feed stopped. This chapter records what happened, what the
product actually computes, how much of it we have reproduced from public
data, what it would cost to run our own, and where the work stands. The
long-form record is `docs/gfds-rebuild-evaluation.md`; every number here is
taken from it or from a committed result file, and the scripts are listed in
`experiments/gfds_rebuild/diagnostics/README.md`.

## What happened

| date | event | evidence |
|---|---|---|
| ~2015 | JRC development ended; the pipeline ran unmaintained | JRC, 2026-09-04 |
| 2025-08-11 | AMSR3 (GOSAT-GW) data record starts at JAXA | JAXA TB catalogue |
| 2026-02-28 | last GFDS GPM file | GDACS listing |
| 2026-03-04 | NASA moves GMI L1B to V08 and from HDF5 to NetCDF4 | NOAA OSPO notice |
| Mar–Sep 2026 | GFDS `ALL` product = AMSR2 only | GDACS listing (byte-identical file sizes) |
| 2026-09-02 | NOAA ends its own AMSR2 processing (AMSR3 transition) | NOAA OSPO |
| 2026-09-14 | **last GFDS file**, a partial day | GDACS listing |
| 2026-10-01 | JAXA G-Portal replaced by a new system (new SFTP host, key-only login) | G-Portal notice |
| 2026-10-22 → 27 | JAXA-wide maintenance; G-Portal unreachable | JAXA notice, our probes |
| 2026-10-26 | JRC's web listings return nothing; the files we had already fetched are our copies | `gdacs_check.py` |
| 2026-11-04 | old G-Portal host shut down (planned); confirmed dead from 2026-10-26 | G-Portal notice |

The GPM stop matches NASA's format change; the AMSR2 stop has no cause in the
data, since JAXA still publishes AMSR2 daily. GFDS died of the thing the
evaluation names as the deciding risk for any replacement: nobody was on call
to absorb upstream changes.

## What GFDS computes

From the 2015 JRC technical note, the whole method fits in one figure. The
input is the 36.5 GHz horizontally polarised brightness temperature, which
water lowers. Each footprint is compared with the warmest dry land around it,
in the swath's own geometry, so physical temperature and atmosphere cancel to
first order.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "The GFDS method, from swath to magnitude. Colours: green = we reproduce JRC's files exactly; amber = close (r 0.8, no bias) from NOAA's data, exact only with JAXA's own calibration; grey = JRC's convention, settled by the answer-key files."
flowchart LR
  A["AMSR2 swath<br/>36.5 GHz H-pol Tb<br/>per footprint M"] --> B["C = 95th percentile<br/>of the 9×9 footprint window<br/>(swath geometry)"]
  A --> C["s = M / C"]
  B --> C
  C --> D["grid 0.09° (4000×2000):<br/>daytime pass first,<br/>night pass fills gaps"]
  D --> E["merge sensors<br/>(ALL = mean of s)"]
  E --> F["magnitude<br/>m = (avg − s) / sd<br/>per-pixel 2002–2008 baseline"]
  F --> G["4-day trailing mean"]
  classDef done fill:#cfe8cf,stroke:#2e7d32;
  classDef close fill:#ffe9b3,stroke:#b26a00;
  classDef conv fill:#e0e0e0,stroke:#616161;
  class F,G done;
  class A,B,C close;
  class D,E conv;
```

Two details are not in the note and had to be found from JRC's own files:
the calibration value is taken among raw footprints, not grid cells, and the
day's grid follows the daytime (ascending) pass where it exists. The note also
writes the magnitude difference the other way round; JRC's files use
avg − s, so a flood gives a positive magnitude.

## How exactly can we reproduce it?

JRC's archive was fully served on 2026-10-26, including per-sensor
"answer-key" files for 2013–2016 (the source Tb, the calibration Tb, the
window position, the signal and the magnitude, each as a daily raster) and
the baseline rasters behind the magnitude. We fetched them
(`gdacs_key_2016.py`); they now live in `data/gdacs_gfds/rebuild/` and on
the team's dev blob under `projects/ds-flood-gfm/raw/gfds/rebuild/`.

**Magnitude: exact.** With JRC's own baseline rasters, our
m = (avg − s)/sd reproduces JRC's magnitude file for 2018-08-20 on 99.9% of
land cells to within the file's 0.001 rounding; the rest is the ±20 clip.
Anyone holding those two rasters and a signal file can produce JRC's
magnitude product exactly.

**Signal: close, not yet exact.** Rebuilding s from NOAA's AMSR2 swath
record (the only AMSR2 archive we could read at the time) and comparing with
JRC's files, West Africa box, land cells (`07_signal_from_swath.py`,
`08_gridding_schemes.py`, `09_window_convention.py`; printed by the scripts,
not loaded here):

| | 2016-08-20 | 2018-08-20 |
|---|---|---|
| our source Tb vs JRC's, UTC-day mean | r 0.77, bias −1.6 K | r 0.75, bias −1.0 K |
| … daytime pass first, night pass fills | r 0.84, bias −0.3 K, MAD 1.1 K | r 0.80, bias −0.4 K, MAD 1.2 K |
| our calibration Tb vs JRC's | r 0.90, MAD 0.65 K | (file empty) |
| our signal s vs JRC's | r 0.74, bias 0.0000, MAD 0.0033 | r 0.56, bias +0.001, MAD 0.0042 |

The residual after the pass rule, about 1.1 K at r 0.8, is the size of the
calibration difference between NOAA's record (tied to GMI) and JAXA's own
L1B, which JRC read. The decisive test is one day of JAXA L1B through
G-Portal (`10_signal_from_jaxa_l1b.py`, written and self-checking). It is
blocked on the G-Portal migration: the new host accepts SSH keys only, and
the key is issued on the website per account.

**Does the inexact signal matter?** For flood tracking, no. At admin level
the rebuilt signal from JAXA's 0.1° grids tracks FloodScan as well as JRC's
combined product did and better than JRC's own AMSR2-only product
(`results/gfds_rebuild/nga2022_lga_r_by_source.csv`, @sec-alternative-sources
for the method). Exactness is a proof point, not a dependency.

## What it would cost to run our own

- **A usable replacement is feasible.** The method is small and fully
  specified, the raw data are public at JAXA, and the rebuilt signal is as
  good as JRC's for flood tracking. What we lose is multi-sensor coverage:
  single-sensor days have swath gaps, so daily land coverage drops from about
  98% to 92% and some cells need the 4-day mean. GFDS is also not FloodScan:
  it gives a flood signal and an anomaly, not a flooded fraction
  (@sec-downscaling-poc and @sec-floodscan-repro are about that gap).
- **Archive, 2012 to now.** About 165 GB of JAXA's daily 0.1° grids, a week
  of downloading at the rates we have seen, compute that runs on a laptop.
  The exact-replica route from raw swaths is about 7 TB, streamed day by day
  rather than kept. Person-time on the order of two to three weeks to build,
  validate against JRC's files and add the flooded-fraction step; the signal
  step is already prototyped.
- **Keeping it current.** AMSR2 still flows from JAXA; its successor AMSR3
  publishes swaths about two hours after acquisition. A daily job is about
  1 GB of input and minutes of compute. The real cost is the dependency:
  one JAXA server, one account, one key, as the October outage showed. That
  single point of failure killed GFDS at JRC, so the budget line that matters
  is someone on call (roughly 0.1–0.2 FTE), not storage or compute.

## Where we are

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Status of the GFDS rebuild, November 2026. Green = done and verified; amber = done but with a known gap; red = blocked on something outside the code."
flowchart TD
  A["JRC archive copied<br/>answer keys, baselines, 2022 signals<br/>backed up to dev blob with sha256 manifest"]:::done
  B["Signal from JAXA L3 grids<br/>gate 1a: flood tracking on par with JRC"]:::done
  C["Signal from NOAA swaths<br/>r 0.8 vs JRC, no bias"]:::amber
  D["Signal from JAXA L1B<br/>script ready; G-Portal key not registered"]:::blocked
  E["Magnitude from JRC baseline<br/>exact"]:::done
  F["Our own baseline (2012–)<br/>needs the L3 archive, ~165 GB"]:::todo
  G["Flooded fraction<br/>crude physics rule only (R1)"]:::amber
  H["Daily job on AMSR3<br/>not started"]:::todo
  B --> C --> D
  B --> E
  B --> F --> H
  G --> H
  classDef done fill:#cfe8cf,stroke:#2e7d32;
  classDef amber fill:#ffe9b3,stroke:#b26a00;
  classDef blocked fill:#f8c9c9,stroke:#c62828;
  classDef todo fill:#ffffff,stroke:#9e9e9e,stroke-dasharray: 4 3;
```

| component | status |
|---|---|
| JRC reference files and baselines | copied before the listings went dark; on blob; may be the only copies |
| daily signal, grid route (JAXA L3) | built and scored (@sec-alternative-sources); the archive fetch needs the new G-Portal key |
| daily signal, swath route | prototype on NOAA data; exact replication pending JAXA L1B |
| magnitude | exact from JRC's baseline |
| flooded fraction | crude rule only; the real work is the FloodScan chain in @sec-floodscan-repro |
| operations | not started; the dependency risk is documented |

**Next steps, in order.** Register the SSH key on the new G-Portal and run
the one-day L1B test (ten minutes each side). Decide whether an exact
replica matters or whether "as good as JRC for flood tracking" is the bar.
Then either fetch the L3 archive for our own baseline, or fold the signal
into the FloodScan-style chain and stop treating GFDS as a separate product.
